title: Euclid's algorithm: remainders, traces and invariants
lead: Find a common divisor by repeatedly replacing a pair with a smaller problem.
why: Euclid's algorithm is a model of algorithmic reasoning: simplify the state while preserving a key property, then explain why the process must terminate.
objectives: Trace the greatest common divisor calculation by hand.
Identify the invariant and termination argument.
Test the implementation with normal and boundary cases.
prerequisites: Nonnegative integers and the remainder operation.

concepts.definition: The greatest positive integer dividing both inputs without a remainder.
For nonnegative a and positive b, a%b is between 0 and b-1.
gcd(a,b) = gcd(b,a mod b), provided b>0.
A sequence of intermediate states such as a,b and remainder.

sections.title: Why remainders make the problem smaller
paragraphs: We could try every possible divisor of 48 and 18, but division tells us that 48 = 2×18 + 12. Any common divisor of 48 and 18 must also divide 12.
Therefore gcd(48,18) equals gcd(18,12), then gcd(12,6), then gcd(6,0). The result is 6. Each transformation preserves the sought divisor.

sections.title: Pseudocode and state transitions
paragraphs: Start with (a,b). While b is not zero, compute r=a mod b, then replace a with b and b with r. The remainder is never computed with divisor zero.
For 48 and 18, the trace reads (48,18,12) → (18,12,6) → (12,6,0) → (6,0). The second component decreases after each iteration.

sections.title: Why the GCD invariant holds
paragraphs: If a number divides both a and b, it also divides a-qb and thus the remainder r. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a=qb+r.
The two pairs have the same common divisors. Once b=0, the current a is the GCD for the stated valid input domain.

sections.title: Why the loop must stop
paragraphs: For nonnegative a and positive b, the remainder is nonnegative and strictly smaller than b. The second component cannot keep decreasing forever without reaching zero.
Inputs (0,18) and (18,0) both have GCD 18. In this teaching contract (0,0) is rejected explicitly because it has no unique greatest positive divisor.

sections.title: Build a safe C++ implementation
paragraphs: Read and validate inputs before the loop. We accept nonnegative values within int range, excluding (0,0). Production-grade code also needs bounds and input-failure handling.
To debug, compare the full trace, not only the last output. Calculate the remainder before overwriting the previous pair.

sections.title: Why the pair replacement preserves the GCD
paragraphs: If a = q·b + r, every common divisor of a and b divides r = a − q·b. Conversely, a common divisor of b and r divides a. Thus the common divisors are unchanged. With b>0, 0≤r<b, so the second value strictly decreases to zero. These arguments establish answer preservation and termination separately. For (18,48), the first remainder is 18; reversed inputs still work.

paragraphs: Laboratory inputs are a,b from 0 to 100000, excluding (0,0). These bounds match the interactive model.

clarity.goal: Find a common divisor by repeatedly replacing a pair with a smaller problem.
prerequisites: You can divide with a remainder and read assignments and a condition. while is introduced here.
model: The greatest common divisor of 48 and 18 is the largest positive number dividing both without a remainder. 48 = 2 × 18 + 12. The common divisors of 48 and 18 are the same as those of 18 and 12: subtracting a multiple preserves them.

While b is not zero, compute a % b, then set a to the old b and b to the remainder. while means repeat while the condition is true; != means not equal. The temporary variable remainder preserves the remainder before a changes.

For b > 0, the remainder is nonnegative and smaller than b. Thus the second number decreases to zero; division by zero never runs because the condition is tested before the body. The pair’s greatest common divisor stays the same at every step: this is the concrete invariant. We do not use the pair 0,0 here.

diagram.caption: Loop pseudocode
diagram.text:
while b ≠ 0:
  r ← a mod b
  a ← b
  b ← r
print a
